--- Page 1 ---
MetaShare: Failure-Aware Collective
Self-Improvement for Open-Ended Agents
Vishal Bhutani
Prasang Gupta
Sumanth Chundru
Kevin Paul
PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC)
{vishal.bhutani, prasang.gupta, sumanth.s.chundru, kevin.x.paul}@pwc.com
Abstract
Humans often learn fastest not by repeating success, but by remembering which
failures not to repeat. Open-ended self-improving agents can share experience
across lineages, as in GEA, or edit their own improvement mechanisms, as in
DGM-Hyperagents, yet failed improvement attempts are rarely retained as reusable
cross-branch knowledge, and search can collapse onto redundant strategies. We
introduce MetaShare, a failure-aware framework that records successful and unsuc-
cessful agent modifications together with signed performance deltas. Before each
generation, MetaShare retrieves diverse high-performing strategies alongside high-
confidence failures from other lineages, letting agents reuse effective mechanisms
while avoiding known dead ends. A task-blind auditor periodically injects absent
or underrepresented mechanism categories, while embedding-based de-ranking
limits redundancy during retrieval. Multiple meta-agents propose modifications in
parallel at heterogeneous temperatures behind a deterministic selector that gates ap-
plicability, scope, compilability, and size. Experiments across paper review, coding,
math grading, robotics reward design, and financial audit-risk assessment show that
MetaShare’s median matches or exceeds DGM-Hyperagents’ final performance
and reaches its own best-performing agent in 1.7–2.9× fewer evolution iterations.
1
Introduction
Open-ended self-improvement asks a system to keep improving the machinery it uses to solve tasks,
not just its answers: a task-agent solves a problem while a meta-agent rewrites the surrounding
scaffold—prompts, tools, memory, and control flow. The Darwin Gödel Machine (DGM) and DGM-
Hyperagents (DGM-H) fold task- and meta-agent into one editable, archive-based program, so the
mechanism that proposes improvements can itself change [Zhang et al., 2025, 2026]; Group-Evolving
Agents (GEA) widen the loop from a single branch to a population whose members inherit one
another’s discoveries [Weng et al., 2026]. Our question is not what these systems search over, but
what they carry forward from one attempt to the next. In DGM-H that is the agent, ranked by a scalar
fitness; its memory can retain regressions, but only within a lineage and in whatever form an agent
happened to record them. GEA broadens who inherits without changing what is inherited: members
exchange agents, trajectories, and patch histories—raw material a later model must re-read before it
can guess which mechanism was responsible. Credit thus lands on the agent, not the mechanism: a
regressing modification leaves only implicit history, so the next meta-agent has no compact, signed
signal for which mechanism to avoid and rediscovers the same dead end, while search narrows as
generation and retrieval reward whatever recently scored well. What is carried forward, in short, is an
agent and a number, not a reusable lesson.
What should it carry forward instead? Human learning suggests the useful unit is not the episode
but the signed lesson: a child who falls learns to stand and then to walk, and an adult who stumbles
recovers in one motion without re-deriving why. We retain that an action helped or hurt, we retain it
40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: Managing Agents that Manage
Agents: Workshop on Responsible Use of Meta-Agents.
arXiv:2610.21887v2  [cs.MA]  19 Nov 2026


--- Page 2 ---
Figure 1: MetaShare converts evaluated outcomes into signed, reusable lessons. A measured scaffold
change becomes a positive (helped, reuse) or negative (hurt, avoid) lesson, passed to generation t+1
to exploit gains and skip known failures.
distilled rather than as a full trace, and we do not keep twenty copies of the same lesson. Those three
properties—signed, distilled, and non-redundant are precisely what a scalar fitness and a raw trace
each fail to supply. Figure 1 shows an evaluated scaffold change becoming exactly such a lesson: a
signed record marked helped or hurt, carried to generation t+1 so that gains are reused and known
dead ends are skipped.
Our approach.
MetaShare supplies these properties by changing the unit of shared experience: each
evaluated self-modification becomes a signed, mechanism-level record—a short, domain-agnostic
description of the mechanism attempted (e.g. “add retry logic for malformed JSON”), its signed
delta, and its provenance—written only after evaluation, so it is an observed outcome rather than a
self-report. Successes and failures are then retrieved through separate channels, a task-blind auditor
injects absent mechanism classes, and several meta-agents propose in parallel behind a deterministic
gate.
Contributions.
• A signed, mechanism-level unit of shared experience. We make the unit of cross-lineage
sharing a signed record of the mechanism attempted, with an explicit avoid-channel for
failures.
• Task-blind search auditing. We steer pool-level search with an auditor that targets
mechanism-class coverage from a scrubbed, leak-checked digest—in contrast to task-aware
reflection, it guides the meta-agent without ever seeing task labels, objectives, or absolute
scores—only signed deltas.
• Failure semantics, isolated. A length-matched shuffled-failure control separates the value
of a failure’s content from the value of extra context, isolating the alignment between a
mechanism and its signed outcome as the source of the gain.
• Cross-domain evidence. One failure-aware mechanism improves search across five het-
erogeneous domains, whereas prior cross-lineage sharing was demonstrated mainly on
coding.
We evaluate MetaShare against DGM-H on the same datasets, models, and evaluators across five
domains—paper review, Polyglot coding, math solution grading, robotics reward design, and a new
financial audit-risk task. It matches or exceeds the baseline’s final quality while converging faster,
and compute-matched ablations attribute the gain to the memory’s structure rather than to added
context or compute.
2
Related Work
Open-ended self-improvement and sharing.
Self-improving systems predate foundation models
[Good, 1966, Schmidhuber, 2003, Kirsch and Schmidhuber, 2022]. Holding weights fixed and
searching the scaffold makes this operational: STOP [Zelikman et al., 2024], ADAS [Hu et al., 2024],
DGM [Zhang et al., 2025], and DGM-H, which folds task- and meta-agent into one editable program
2


--- Page 3 ---
Figure 2: MetaShare architecture. Top: one generation—select parent ap, build the signed-guidance
context Cg (adopt/avoid/must-try), let K meta-agents propose patches, admit one through a determin-
istic gate, then apply and score it to yield ac. Bottom: each evaluated modification becomes a signed
record in a bounded cross-lineage pool; failure-aware diverse retrieval rebuilds Cg, and a task-blind
auditor injects Must-Try classes from a scrubbed digest.
[Zhang et al., 2026]. GEA shares experience across a population rather than a lineage [Weng et al.,
2026]; ExpeL distills insights from trajectories [Zhao et al., 2024]; Reflexion and Self-Refine reuse
the sign of feedback [Shinn et al., 2024, Madaan et al., 2023]. MetaShare changes what is inherited: a
persistent, signed, mechanism-level record indexed by outcome across lineages, rather than an agent
archive or free-form reflection.
Diversity-preserving search.
Novelty search rewards behavioral difference over progress toward a
fixed objective [Lehman and Stanley, 2011], and quality–diversity methods such as MAP-Elites retain
strong solutions across niches [Mouret and Clune, 2015]. MetaShare borrows this intuition without
a QD archive: a task-blind auditor targets mechanism-category coverage rather than ranking by
score, and embedding de-ranking—related to maximal marginal relevance [Carbonell and Goldstein,
1998]—reduces redundancy among retrieved modification records.
Parallel generation and selection.
Self-consistency shows the value of sampling and aggregating
multiple reasoning paths [Wang et al., 2022]; MetaShare transfers the multiple-sample idea to
code modifications via parallel meta-agents at heterogeneous temperatures. Rather than a learned
judge—which carries position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases [Zheng et al., 2023]—it
admits candidates by deterministic checks (applicability, scope, compilation, size), leaving quality to
empirical evaluation.
3
Method
We define meta-strategy memory as the persistent storage and retrieval of evaluated improvement
strategies, each summarizing the mechanism attempted, its measured effect, and its archive prove-
nance. It is language-based because a self-modification’s reusable content often lies at the mechanism
level: a long diff may instantiate the same idea as “add retry logic for malformed JSON outputs.”
Figure 2 shows how recording (Sec. 3.1), failure-aware retrieval (Sec. 3.2), diversity control and
auditing (Sec. 3.3), and proposal selection (Sec. 3.4) compose into one evolution generation.
3.1
Signed Meta-Strategy Records
At generation g, a parent agent ap = (Tp, Mp), with task-agent Tp and meta-agent Mp, is selected
from the archive Ag. Given permitted history Hg and retrieved MetaShare context Cg, the meta-agent
proposes a patch pg, which is applied to produce a child:
pg = M(ap, Hg, Cg),
ac = Apply(ap, pg).
(1)
The child transition in Eq. 1 is evaluated on the domain task, and only afterward can MetaShare write
to the pool: a record is thus an evaluated transition with a known outcome, not a self-report of intent.
3


--- Page 4 ---
The update fires whenever a generation yields a non-empty diff and at least one valid score; it extracts
the diff, computes parent and child scores, and classifies and summarizes the diff into a reusable
mechanism description.
Formally, for evaluator score q(a; D), MetaShare converts the parent–child transition into a signed
meta-strategy record:
si = (∆i, ci, ri, δi, qp
i , qc
i ,
di, ℓi, gi),
δi = qc
i −qp
i .
(2)
Here ∆i is the modification (task-agent, meta-agent, or both), ci its mechanism type, ri a concise
description, δi the signed performance change, qp
i , qc
i parent and child scores, di the domain, ℓi
the source-parent identifier, and gi the generation. Type and description come from a post-hoc
classification step; the type drives retrieval diversity and auditing, preventing domination by one
family and letting the auditor spot underexplored classes. The fixed vocabulary is prompt engineering,
tool creation, memory, evaluation logic, self-modification, and structural refactoring. Each record
thus separates what was attempted, what happened, and where, without exposing benchmark labels
or traces.
MetaShare accumulates these records into a persistent strategy pool Pg = {s1, s2, . . . }, the set of all
signed records written through generation g. The sign of the delta δi then splits the pool into positive
and non-positive evidence:
P+
g = {si ∈Pg : δi > 0}, P−
g = {si ∈Pg : δi ≤0}
(3)
so P+
g holds the mechanisms that improved performance (candidates to reuse) and P−
g holds those
that did not (explicit avoid-signals). Persisting each record makes the outcome available outside its
originating branch, so later meta-agents retrieve an attempt’s description, sign, and provenance rather
than rediscovering it. The pool is capacity-bounded at 100 records; on overflow the lowest-delta
records are evicted first, so the most negative failures go before any success. Each generation writes
at most one record, so only the 200-generation IMO runs can reach the bound.
3.2
Failure-Aware Retrieval
Before each generation, MetaShare turns the pool into a prompt context with two goals: expose the
parent to mechanisms found outside its source branch, and present failures as explicit evidence, not
buried log history. Since ℓi is the source-parent identifier, filtering out records with ℓi = ℓp yields
the eligible pool ePg (with positive and non-positive parts eP+
g and eP−
g ): a conservative parent-level
exclusion that encourages cross-source transfer rather than full ancestry removal.
Retrieval is deliberately asymmetric: positive records are candidate mechanisms to adapt, non-positive
records are constraints and warnings. From the eligible pool, MetaShare selects the two sets actually
placed in the meta-agent’s context—the retrieved positives S+
g and the retrieved failures S−
g —under
a positive budget Ks and a failure budget Kf:
S+
g = DiverseTopK( eP+
g , Ks),
S−
g = BottomK( eP−
g , Kf),
(4)
Here DiverseTopK returns the highest-δi positives, diversified across mechanism types (Sec. 3.3),
and BottomK returns the most negative (worst) failures; so S+
g supplies mechanisms to adapt and
S−
g mechanisms to avoid or revise. By default Ks = 5, with up to Kf = 5 worst failures appended
after the positives.
The formatted context preserves the sign of the evidence—positives as strategies to adopt, failures in
a separate section labeled as reducing performance—so the meta-agent gets a compact mechanism
description with its outcome’s direction and magnitude, not a long trace to interpret.
3.3
Diversity Control and Search Audit
Failure-aware retrieval avoids repeating known bad strategies but does not prevent collapse onto a
few high-scoring recipes: if recent gains come mostly from prompt edits, a delta-ranked retriever may
4


--- Page 5 ---
surface several prompt variants and little on tools, memory, evaluation logic, or self-modification.
MetaShare therefore adds three layers.
The first is category-aware retrieval. After ranking positives by delta, MetaShare takes at most one
representative per strategy type before filling the remaining budget by score, using the type field ci as
a control variable, not a descriptive afterthought.
The second is semantic de-ranking. Each positive strategy is embedded from its description and
added patch lines, with similarity measured by cosine; strategies above threshold τ are grouped and
the highest-delta member preferred. Running this at retrieval, not storage, lets the pool keep related
attempts for analysis while the prompt avoids redundant paraphrases, preserving useful variation
[Lehman and Stanley, 2011, Mouret and Clune, 2015, Pugh et al., 2016] without behavioral niches or
a QD score.
The third is a task-blind search audit. Every C generations it receives a scrubbed digest of strategy
types, signed deltas, and added lines—task identifiers, benchmark names, and other domain-revealing
patterns removed—and names absent or underrepresented mechanism classes. It does not see the
task, rank agents, or solve anything.
The output is used only if it passes a leak check against the same policy—scanned for the blocked
tokens and patterns above and, on detection, retried once, else rejected. A valid audit is prepended to
later contexts as a MUST-TRY directive—the cached directive ug of Algorithm 1—and an invalid
one is discarded with the prior valid directive retained. Together the three layers separate two
often-conflated goals: reusing what worked and keeping the improvement policy from narrowing too
early.
3.4
Proposal Generation, Selection, and Update
After building the context, the system decides which self-modification to evaluate. MetaShare can
sample several candidates for the same parent:
pg,k = Mθk(ap, Hg, Cg),
k ∈{1, . . . , K}.
(5)
Each of the K proposals runs in an independent container and repo copy; temperatures θk are specified
or spread uniformly over [0.3, 0.9]. Only one is evaluated, so extra proposals raise self-modification
cost but not domain-evaluation cost.
The selector is structural, not predictive. For candidate patch p,
V (p) = Iapply(p) Iscope(p) Icompile(p) Isize(p),
Isize(p) = 1[ 5 ≤L(p) ≤300 ].
(6)
requiring clean application, allowed scope, successful Python compilation, and a bounded line count;
any failed gate disqualifies the patch, and ties are broken by a generation-seeded random choice. This
keeps a learned judge out of candidate selection while evaluation measures quality; the post-hoc
classifier and the auditor are language models, but neither ranks candidates.
The selected patch is applied and screened on a low-cost subset, with full evaluation run only when
the staged score exceeds γ. Values for γ, the de-ranking threshold τ, the audit cadence C, the pool
capacity bound, and the embedding model are listed per domain in Appendix A. The evaluated child
enters the archive, and the post-evaluation update turns the transition into a signed record. Algorithm 1
summarizes the loop: retrieval builds the context, proposals generate candidates, selection picks one
patch, and evaluation updates both archive and strategy memory.
4
Experiments and Results
The experiments compare MetaShare against DGM-H on the same datasets, models, and evaluators,
asking whether it matches or improves DGM-H’s best performance RQ1 (final quality) and whether
it reaches comparable quality in fewer generations or tokens RQ2 (search efficiency). Ablations
then isolate which parts of the memory and retrieval pipeline account for the gains.
5


--- Page 6 ---
Algorithm 1 MetaShare evolution
Require: initial agent a0, budget G, proposal count K
1: A0 ←{a0}, P0 ←∅
2: for g = 1, . . . , G do
3:
Select parent ap from Ag−1; load cached audit ug
4:
if audit is due then
5:
Scrub Pg−1, run blind audit, leak-check ug
6:
end if
7:
Retrieve S+
g , S−
g from Pg−1; form context Cg with ug
8:
Generate K patches {pg,k}; select valid p⋆
g
9:
if no valid patch then
10:
Ag ←Ag−1, Pg ←Pg−1; continue
11:
end if
12:
Apply p⋆
g to get child ac; evaluate to obtain qc
13:
Ag ←Ag−1 ∪{ac}
14:
Build record sg from p⋆
g, q(ap), qc; insert into Pg
15: end for
16: return AG, PG
4.1
Dataset
Our evaluation spans five domains: four inherited unchanged from the DGM-H suite—enabling direct
comparison against the self-improving-agent baseline—and one new financial audit-risk task that we
curate (described below).
Inherited domains.
For the four inherited domains we adopt the datasets, splits, and model
configurations of DGM-H and refer the reader to Zhang et al. [2026] for their full specification,
summarizing each only briefly here. Paper review is a binary accept/reject task over research papers,
testing long-context, criteria-based judgment. Polyglot coding evaluates code generation across
languages on a unique 225 coding tasks. Mathematical solution grading (IMO) grades Olympiad-
level solutions—scored by exact accuracy and normalized mean absolute error (NMAE)—in three
settings: IMO (init), IMO (transfer), and IMO (full). Robotics reward design evaluates generated
reward functions for quadruped locomotion by average fitness. Except for Polyglot, each uses disjoint
train/validation/test splits, with the validation-selected checkpoint evaluated once on the held-out test
set.
Financial audit-risk assessment.
Beyond the four inherited benchmarks, we curate an audit-risk
dataset from the financial disclosures of 15 real audit clients, testing whether MetaShare transfers to
a document-grounded setting rather than only to the tasks it was tuned alongside. For each client we
assess the 15 Inherent Risk Factors (IRFs) defined in the audit domain, giving 225 labelled (client,
IRF) pairs under a client-level split (8 train, 2 validation, 5 test), so the test fold is 75 decisions
clustered within five filings. Given chunks of a client’s 10-K Financial Notes and an IRF, the task
predicts one of three risk levels—High, Medium, or None—and we let the framework discover
the mapping rather than supplying a hand-specified rule, so accuracy measures agreement with
expert judgement rather than audit-grade assessment. Because skewed labels can make surface-
level predictions look correct, we report overall accuracy, normalized mean absolute error, and
per-risk-factor accuracy; per-IRF definitions are in Appendix F.1.
4.2
Results
We compare MetaShare with DGM-H on the same datasets, splits, models, and evaluators. For
paper review, robotics, and the three IMO settings, DGM-H scores, intervals, and generations-to-
best are those reported by Zhang et al. [2026]; we did not rerun them, so on these domains our
admissibility gate (Sec. 3.4) is not held fixed across arms. For Polyglot and audit risk, the baseline
is our reimplementation—MetaShare with the pool disabled and a single meta-agent (k=1), same
gate—so the difference spans the memory-and-retrieval layer and parallel proposal generation, not a
change of agent or evaluator; the ablations (Sec. 5) attribute gains to individual components. Every
6


--- Page 7 ---
Figure 3: MetaShare vs. DGM-H across all evaluation domains. Left: final score (↑); right: generation
of the selected best (↓), with per-domain speed-up. Error bars are 95% bootstrap CIs where available.
DGM-H values for paper review, robotics, and IMO (scores, intervals, and generations) are as
reported by Zhang et al. [2026], not rerun; the Polyglot and audit-risk DGM-H bars are our five-run
reimplementation. Dashed lines mark the static, no-self-improvement baseline [Zhang et al., 2026,
Luong et al., 2025] (none for Polyglot or audit risk). NMAE (↓) is 0.175 vs. 0.157 (IMO-full)
and 0.357 vs. 0.312 (audit risk). For Polyglot both arms hold the task-agent on o3-mini here, with
the DGM-H baseline rerun on a Sonnet-4.5 meta-agent (Sonnet-3.5 deprecated); Sec. 5.2 analyzes
model-routing separately.
condition we run is run five times, following DGM-H’s protocol. GEA’s released harness is coding-
specific and reports no numbers on our other domains, so we compare against it only on Polyglot,
under its own protocol.
We report medians over five runs with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, generations to the
best checkpoint, and token cost. Figure 3 summarizes the comparison across all five domains:
MetaShare matches or exceeds DGM-H’s final quality while converging in far fewer generations.
Median score improves on paper review (0.71 →0.79), Polyglot (0.28 →0.34, full 225 tasks,
backbone held on o3-mini), robotics reward design (0.37→0.40), the three IMO-grading settings
(0.61/0.64/0.60 →0.64/0.70/0.67), and audit risk (0.45 →0.55), while the generation at which
the selected best appears falls by 1.7–2.9× (e.g. 100 →36 on paper review and 44 →26 on audit
risk). This locates each arm’s best checkpoint rather than timing arrival at a fixed target, and on paper
review the baseline’s best coincides with its budget, so that ratio is a lower bound.
On the small and medium set of 60 tasks in Polyglot benchmark, GEA reports 0.88 from a single run
(Claude Sonnet-4.5 as both task- and meta-agent); matching that configuration, MetaShare reaches
0.917 [0.900, 0.933] over five runs within 10 iterations. A five-run interval and a single point estimate
are not like-for-like, so we read this as competitive at a lower iteration count rather than a win; per-run
detail is in Appendix G.1.
We follow DGM-H’s accounting protocol [Zhang et al., 2026]: only the self-modification term differs,
since the task-evaluation term is identical per iteration. Running k=3 meta-agents makes MetaShare’s
self-modification about 3× the single-agent baseline, but total cost stays within the same order of
magnitude because evaluation dominates and is independent of k. Table 1 gives the totals: MetaShare
is the more expensive method on two of the three domains we account for.
5
Ablation Studies
The ablations test whether MetaShare’s gains come from the structure of the memory rather than
from added context or compute. We ask two questions: AQ1 (failure semantics)—does the content
of a failure record help beyond the prompt tokens it adds?—and AQ2 (search auditing)—does
the task-blind auditor broaden the meta-agent’s search instead of letting it collapse onto redundant

5.1
Component Ladder (Paper Review)
We toggle one component at a time on paper review, holding base system, model, domain, protocol,
and five paired runs fixed; Table 2 reports best-so-far accuracy (median, 95% bootstrap CI) and
generations-to-best. Every component helps, and the two splits agree. The signed failure channel
adds +0.02/+0.04 (train/val), so negative records carry usable avoid-signals, not merely extra
tokens (AQ1); parallel heterogeneous proposals give the largest ladder step; and the task-blind auditor
completes the system (AQ2). A k=3 generation costs about 3× the self-modification tokens (Table 1),
so this is a quality-and-speed gain, not a token-efficiency claim.
The ladder adds parallel proposals partway up, so it cannot separate the memory layer from proposal
count. A compute-matched reference—the pool disabled at k=3, same gate, temperature spread,
budget, and paired runs (last row of Table 2)—reaches 0.72 [.72, .73] val in 55 generations. At
identical proposal count the memory layer and auditor therefore account for +0.11 val and 19 fewer
generations, disjoint from the full system’s 0.83 [.80, .88]; signed memory alone supplies +0.06 (also
disjoint), the auditor +0.05. The large k=1 →k=3 ladder step is thus not evidence that proposal
count drives the result: at matched count the memory layer accounts for the gain, and Sec. 5.2 repeats
the comparison on Polyglot, where proposal count alone contributes nothing.
5.2
Failure Semantics and Auditing (Polyglot)
On Polyglot we separate the two questions with single-component removals from the full k=3 system
(Table 3). Replacing true failure records with length-matched shuffled failures costs 0.07: the gain
comes from the semantics of a failure, not from the extra prompt tokens (AQ1). Removing the task-
blind auditor costs 0.15 (AQ2), which splits into its search effect under a fixed backbone (0.30→0.34,
matching the 0.04/0.05 train/val on paper review) and the routing it unlocks (0.34→0.45, below).
With the pool disabled at k=3 the system reaches only the k=1 baseline’s 0.28 (Table 3), so the k=3
advantage comes from the memory layer, not the extra proposals.
Auditor-induced dynamic model selection.
On Polyglot the auditor unlocks a capability rather
than an incremental gain. Both arms begin every run from an identical GPT o3-mini backbone under

meta-agent upgrades the task-agent to GPT 4o-mini—reproducibly across runs, whereas DGM-H,
with the identical ability, never proposes it and stays on o3-mini (direct evidence for AQ2). Since this
model change is an uncontrolled difference between the arms, we note that runs keeping o3-mini
throughout still beat the DGM-H baseline in fewer iterations (Figure 3).
6
Conclusion and Future Work
MetaShare makes each evaluated self-modification a signed, mechanism-level strategy, retrieved
through separate success and failure channels under a task-blind auditor. Across five domains
it matches or exceeds DGM-H’s quality while reaching its own best agent in 1.7–2.9× fewer
generations, at token cost within the same order of magnitude. Compute-matched ablations locate the
gain in the memory’s structure rather than added compute, and the auditor additionally induces a
model-routing strategy the baseline never proposes.
Limitations and future work.
Mechanism type and description come from an unvalidated LLM
classifier. Results rest on five runs with often-overlapping CIs, so efficiency is the robust signal;
type-diverse retrieval and de-ranking are not independently ablated. Only Polyglot and audit risk
rerun DGM-H behind our gate; the other domains use its published numbers. The gate, retrieval
rules, and auditor cadence are fixed scaffolding rather than evolved, and the size band is not ablated;
DGM-H never discovering the routing strategy (Sec. 5.2) suggests some useful structure does not
emerge unaided, but letting a hyperagent evolve this machinery is future work. The audit-risk corpus
is internal (Appendix F.2). Extensions include cross-branch pollination and an adaptive auditor
cadence.
7
Responsible-Use Statement
MetaShare is a research artifact, not a deployable agent: it accelerates search toward whatever the
domain evaluator encodes and can amplify misspecification in that evaluator, so we intend it only
for supervised, sandboxed settings with a bounded action space and an accountable human owner.
Reaching the best agent in 1.7–2.9× fewer generations compresses the oversight window, so we
recommend budgeting inspection per unit of change rather than per iteration and treating exercised
rollback and halt—native to the archive—as a precondition for larger budgets. Cross-lineage sharing
propagates errors as readily as gains: an unvalidated post-hoc classifier can misdirect retrieval
population-wide, and a failure channel scored on a single scalar can persist caution-improving
mechanisms as avoid-signals; deployments should exempt designated classes from the negative
channel or score them under a separate objective. The task-blind auditor is a leakage control, not a
safety control—Must-Try directives should be logged, treated as untrusted, and deny-listed—and the
real bound is the sandboxed action space, not the gate, as when the auditor induced an unanticipated
but permitted backbone switch. The audit-risk corpus uses public 10-K notes with expert labels,
contains no personal data, and is not released; accuracy is agreement with expert judgement rather than
audit-grade assessment, locomotion rewards are simulation-only, and we do not endorse automating
peer-review decisions.
9

Appendix
This appendix provides supporting material referenced by the main text: implementation settings,
prompts, the admissibility gate, compute and randomization protocol, the audit-risk dataset, and
Polyglot per-run detail.
A
Implementation and Hyperparameter Settings
The main paper points here for five values: the staged-evaluation threshold γ, the de-ranking threshold
τ, the audit cadence C, the pool capacity bound and the embedding model. Of these, γ and τ are
the two that are set per domain, and they are listed per domain in Table 5 together with the decoding
temperatures; C, the pool bound and the embedding model took the same value in every domain and
are listed once in Table 4 rather than repeated across five identical rows.
With two exceptions the settings below are either inherited or left at their defaults. The exceptions
are the de-ranking threshold τ, chosen between two candidate values on one or two dry runs, and
the decoding temperatures, which were set per domain. The staged-evaluation protocol is inherited
from DGM-Hyperagents [Zhang et al., 2026] so that the comparison against that baseline holds the
evaluation protocol fixed. No value was selected on the basis of held-out test performance.

Staged evaluation.
Each generated agent is first scored on a low-cost screen and proceeds to
full evaluation only if that score clears a threshold γ. The screen sizes are inherited from DGM-
Hyperagents throughout: 10 →100 tasks for paper review and IMO grading, 3 →6 repetitions
for robotics, and 10 →+50 for Polyglot. Polyglot is also the one domain where γ takes a positive
value (0.4), and the one where the screen and the full evaluation come from the same pool of
tasks rather than from separate splits: an agent is first run on 10 tasks and, if it solves at least 4
of them, on the remaining 50, giving 60 in total. The generation that scores best over those 60
tasks is the checkpoint evaluated on all 225, as described below. For the other inherited domains
DGM-Hyperagents specifies failure by example, as scoring nothing on the screen (predicting no paper
review correctly, or producing no compilable reward function), which gives γ = 0. We apply that
same convention to IMO grading, for which no explicit criterion is given, and to our own audit-risk
domain; the resulting per-domain values of γ are collected in Table 5. Polyglot has no validation split,
so its results are development-selected; the other domains select on validation and touch the held-out
test set once.
Polyglot also separates the set the search runs against from the set the results are reported on. Every
generation of the evolution loop is scored on the 60-task small+medium subset, and that score is
what parent selection, the strategy pool’s signed deltas and the auditor’s digest are all computed
from. The accuracies the main paper reports on the full 225-task benchmark are obtained afterwards:
the best-scoring generation under that development score is taken and evaluated once on all 225
tasks. The 60-task subset is contained in those 225 tasks, so the reported figure covers the subset
the checkpoint was selected on as well as the 165 tasks held back from the search; this is what it
11


--- Page 12 ---
means for Polyglot’s results to be development-selected rather than measured on a disjoint split. Any
score quoted from inside a run — such as the pool deltas traced in Sec. G.4 — is therefore a 60-task
development score and is not commensurable with the 225-task figures.
Meta-agent sampling temperatures.
The K parallel meta-agents are differentiated by decoding
temperature, supplied explicitly per run and set per domain; Table 5 lists the values. The main paper
describes these temperatures as either specified or spread uniformly over [0.3, 0.9]: the uniform
spread is the fallback that applies when a run supplies no temperatures, and every run reported here
supplied them explicitly, so the table gives the values actually used rather than that fallback. The
configurations differ in their exact temperatures but share a common shape at K=3: a greedy decode
at 0.0 paired with a moderate and an exploratory slot. Because the greedy slot is always present, the
K=3 arm contains the K=1 proposal as its first slot and strictly adds two stochastic proposals, rather
than trading determinism for stochasticity. A single-proposal configuration (K=1) therefore runs at
0.0.
The assignment is across slots, not across generations: the same triple is used in every generation,
so the diversity it supplies is between the simultaneous proposals within a generation rather than a
schedule that anneals from exploration toward exploitation as a run progresses.

A.1
Values Tried During Development
Three settings were varied while developing the system. The proposal count was swept over k ∈
{1, 3}; that sweep is not hidden here but reported as the component ladder in the ablation of the
main paper, so its effect can be read directly off the results. The de-ranking threshold τ was chosen
between 0.85 and 0.92 on the basis of one or two short dry runs, and the value that each domain then
ran with is listed in Table 5. The decoding temperatures were set per domain (Table 5), always as a
greedy slot paired with a moderate and an exploratory one, rather than searched over a grid.
Every other value was fixed before the reported runs. The staged threshold γ and the screen sizes are
inherited from DGM-Hyperagents, and the auditor cadence C, the pool bound, the retrieval budgets
Ks and Kf, the token budget and the embedding model were left at their defaults. In no case was a
setting chosen using held-out test performance: the dry runs behind τ were short and were judged
on training-side behaviour only, and the test split of each domain was evaluated once, for the finally
selected checkpoint.
B
Prompts
This section reproduces the prompts for the three LLM-driven components of the system, as described
in the main paper. Text in braces (for example {repo_path}) marks a format field substituted at
call time; angle-bracketed text marks a value rendered at run time. Em dashes in the originals are
transcribed here as --.
Each exhibit is colour-coded by component, reusing the palette of the architecture figure in the main
paper: grey for the inherited base loop, blue for MetaShare’s memory, orange for the task-blind
auditor, and green for the post-hoc record classifier. Inside an exhibit, a prompt’s own delimiter lines
are set in the accent colour so that its scaffolding separates from its instruction text, and a ,→marks a
line wrapped to fit the page rather than a line break present in the original.
12


--- Page 13 ---
B.1
Task-Agent Prompt
The main paper describes the task-agent as the component that solves the target task. The initial
task-agent carries no domain knowledge and no solution strategy; every capability reported in the
paper is acquired by evolution rather than supplied here. This is the prompt of the unmodified starting
agent.
Prompt 1: Task-agent. Prompt carried by the unmodified initial agent.
You are an agent.
Task input:
‘‘‘
{inputs}
‘‘‘
Respond in JSON format with the following schema:
<json>
{
"response": ...
}
</json>
B.2
Meta-Agent Prompt
The meta-agent proposes a patch from the parent agent, its permitted history, and the retrieved context,
as formalised in “Signed Meta-Strategy Records” in the main paper. The base instruction is a single
line:
Prompt 2: Meta-agent. Base instruction. With the shared strategy pool disabled, this single line is
the entire baseline prompt.
Modify any part of the codebase at ‘{repo_path}‘.
This single line is also exactly the prompt used by the baseline: with the shared strategy pool disabled
no further text is appended, so the only difference in the meta-agent’s prompt is the retrieved context
added below. The baseline additionally runs at k=1, as the main paper states, so the two systems differ
in proposal count as well; the compute-matched arm of the main paper’s ablation is the comparison
that holds that count fixed.
When retrieved strategies are available, the following block is appended:
Prompt 3: Meta-agent. Block appended to the prompt when retrieved strategies are available.
=== SHARED META-STRATEGIES FROM OTHER BRANCHES ===
The following meta-agent modifications were discovered by other
evolutionary branches and led to performance improvements:
{shared_strategies}
You may adopt, adapt, or ignore these strategies based on your
own assessment. Focus on what will most improve this specific agent.
===
Structure of the retrieved context.
The {shared_strategies} field is assembled under an
approximate 20k-token budget and realises the signed channels described under “Failure-Aware
Retrieval”: positive records are presented as mechanisms to adopt or adapt, and non-positive records
13


--- Page 14 ---
appear in a separate section explicitly labelled as reducing performance. Blocks appear in the
following order, and each is emitted only when applicable.
Prompt 4: Meta-agent. Structure of the retrieved context that fills the shared-strategies field. Each
block is emitted only when applicable.
--- MUST TRY: mechanism categories absent from all prior strategies (eval-blind audit) ---
You MUST attempt one of the categories below. Do not produce another variation of the
,→recipes shown later -- that path has plateaued.
<auditor output: 6-10 numbered mechanism categories>
--- PRIOR STRATEGIES (reference only -- do NOT clone the dominant recipe) ---
[Strategy 1] +0.001234 on <domain> (gen_<N>, branch <lineage_id>):
<mechanism description>
--- STRATEGIES THAT REDUCED PERFORMANCE or DID NOT WORK (avoid these approaches)---
[Strategy 2] -0.004500 on <domain> (gen_<N>, branch <lineage_id>):
<mechanism description>
--- UNEXPLORED STRATEGY DIRECTIONS: <mechanism types absent from the pool> ---
NOTE: ’<type>’ strategies show diminishing returns (<k>/<n> entries, avg recent delta: <
,→value>). Consider fundamentally different approaches such as architectural changes,
,→
adding retry logic, or creating new tools.
Each record is rendered with its signed delta, its domain, its generation, its branch of origin, and the
distilled mechanism description. The positive and non-positive channels are properties of the pool
itself, so they are present in every arm that retains the pool, independently of the auditor.
The domain field di is a provenance tag rather than part of the lesson: it is written after evaluation,
together with the signed delta, and is rendered so that a retrieved record carries the origin of the
attempt alongside its outcome. The main paper’s description of a record as a compact, domain-
agnostic lesson refers to the mechanism description ri, which names only the mechanism attempted
and carries no task text, no ground-truth answers and no execution trace. Task-blindness is a property
of the auditor path and not of this context: the digest sent to the auditor is assembled separately and
carries no domain field at all (Sec. B.5).
The last two blocks are likewise independent of the auditor, and the difference in kind between them
and the MUST-TRY block is what the auditor ablation isolates. The unexplored-directions line is a
set difference against the fixed six-label vocabulary of Table 7: it can name a label that has not yet
appeared, but it cannot describe a mechanism, contrast one against what the pool already holds, or
propose anything outside those six labels. The saturation note is a single fixed sentence, emitted
when one label accounts for more than 80% of a pool of at least five records and the mean delta of
that label’s five most recent records is below 0.05. The MUST-TRY block is the only channel that
reads the diffs themselves and returns novel, free-form mechanism categories, each with a structural
contrast against the pool and an optional code-pattern hint, under instruction to attempt one of them.
Removing the auditor therefore leaves a coarse coverage hint over six fixed labels in place while
removing the semantic gap analysis. This also explains why dynamic model selection could only
have originated with the auditor: changing which model the task-agent uses is not expressible in the
six-label vocabulary.
B.3
The Shuffled-Failure Control
The failure-semantics ablation of the main paper replaces true failure records with length-matched
shuffled ones, so that the arm keeps whatever a failure channel contributes as prompt tokens while
destroying the information it carries. That comparison is only interpretable if the two arms differ in
exactly one respect, so we record here what the control holds fixed and what it perturbs.
14


--- Page 15 ---
Held fixed.
The failure block is emitted in the same position in the context, under the same heading,
at the same budget Kf, and with the same per-entry rendering as the full system: a signed delta, the
domain, the generation, the branch of origin, and a mechanism description. The positive channel
S+
g , the auditor directive, the unexplored-directions footer and every other block of Prompt 4 are
untouched, and the arm runs at the same k, the same decoding temperatures and the same five paired
run configurations as the full system.
Perturbed.
The mechanism descriptions are permuted across the whole non-positive pool P −
g , not
only across the Kf records that reach the prompt, so a retrieved failure may carry the description of
any non-positive record in the pool. Each entry is therefore shown against a delta and a provenance
that are not its own, and permuting over the wider pool makes it unlikely that an entry is returned its
own description by chance.
Because descriptions are permuted rather than replaced with generated filler, the block keeps its
entry count exactly and its length in distribution: every description the meta-agent reads is still a real
description of a real modification, drawn from the same population and therefore of the same kind
and typical length as the one it displaces. This is the sense in which the control is length-matched. It
spends the same prompt budget on the same kind of text, and differs from the full system only in
whether that text describes the record it is attached to.
What this isolates.
The arm therefore holds constant the presence of a failure section, its entry
count, its formatting and its token cost up to the per-entry variation just described, and varies only
whether a mechanism description is aligned with the outcome it actually produced. A drop under
this control is evidence that the alignment between a mechanism and its signed outcome is what the
meta-agent uses, rather than the extra context a failure channel supplies.
B.4
Task-Blind Auditor Prompt
The auditor is the third layer of the search audit described in the main paper. It receives only
mechanism-type labels, signed deltas, and scrubbed added lines, and it is told explicitly that it does
not know the domain, the tasks, or what a delta means in absolute terms. Its output is leak-checked
before any of it reaches the meta-agent.
Prompt 5: Auditor. Task-blind gap-audit prompt.
You are auditing a pool of {n} code diffs that modify a self-improving agent’s source
,→files. You will see only the added lines from each diff, plus an abstract "
,→strategy type" label and a numeric "delta" (improvement vs parent on some unknown
,→evaluation).
You DO NOT know:
- What domain the agent is solving
- What tasks were used to score it
- What "delta" represents in absolute terms
- What languages, libraries, or task content are involved
You DO see: {n} diffs of agent code changes (the diffs themselves, scrubbed of domain
,→identifiers).
POOL CONTENTS (each entry shows scrubbed added-lines from one diff):
{pool}
YOUR JOB: Identify mechanism CATEGORIES that are absent or under-represented in this pool
,→of agent-improvement strategies. Give your answer as a list of generic, domain-
,→agnostic mechanism categories that would expand the search space.
Constraints:
- Output mechanism CATEGORIES only (e.g., "multi-sample self-consistency"), NOT specific
,→tasks, languages, or domain references
- The output will be shown to a meta-agent that should NOT learn anything about the eval
,→set from your suggestions
15


--- Page 16 ---
- Keep each category abstract enough that it applies to any code-modification or reasoning
,→
task
Format your output as a numbered list of 6-10 mechanism categories. For each:
- The category name
- A 1-2 sentence description of how it would differ STRUCTURALLY from any of the {n} diffs
,→
above
- Optionally: a code-pattern hint (e.g., "introduces a ‘vote()‘ function over K samples")
,→-- but no domain references
Do not include task names, language names, or eval discussion. Mechanism categories only.
What the auditor actually receives.
The {pool} field is built from a pool snapshot in which every
diff is reduced to its added lines and then scrubbed of domain identifiers. Each entry is rendered as:
Prompt 6: Auditor. Per-entry format of the scrubbed pool digest supplied to the auditor.
=== ENTRY [<id>] type=<mechanism type> delta=<+0.00> ===
<scrubbed added lines from the diff>

B.5
Scrubbing and Leak Check
The main paper states that the auditor is sent a digest with task identifiers, benchmark names, language
names, file extensions, evaluation ratios and other domain-revealing patterns removed, and that its
output is admitted only if it passes a leak check against the same policy. This section gives that policy
explicitly, so the claim can be checked rather than taken on trust.
Interface.
Three functions implement the policy:
forbidden_set(subsets_dir: Optional[str], mode: str) -> Tuple[List[str], List[str]]
scrub(text: str, tokens: List[str], patterns: List[str]) -> str
leak_check(text: str, tokens: List[str], patterns: List[str]) -> Tuple[bool, Optional[str
,→]]
forbidden_set returns a list of literal tokens and a list of regular expressions. Tokens are matched
case-insensitively on word boundaries, so ts does not match inside tests; the patterns are applied
as regular expressions. scrub replaces every match with the literal string DOMAIN, longest token first
so that a short token cannot consume part of a longer one, and is applied to the added lines of each
16


--- Page 17 ---
diff before the audit call. leak_check runs the same search over the auditor’s output and returns the
first offending phrase, if any.
Policy contents.
Task identifiers are loaded from the domain’s subsets directory, so they follow
whatever that domain defines rather than being hard-coded. The remainder of the policy is fixed:
_STATIC_DOMAIN_TOKENS = [
’polyglot’, ’paper-review’, ’paperreview’,
’exercism’, ’testbed’, ’swebench’, ’swe-bench’,
’humaneval’, ’mbpp’, ’apps benchmark’,
]
_STATIC_LANGUAGE_TOKENS = [
’python’, ’rust’, ’java’, ’javascript’, ’js’, ’golang’, ’go ’,
’c++’, ’cpp’, ’kotlin’, ’ruby’, ’swift’, ’typescript’, ’ts ’,
’php’, ’scala’, ’haskell’, ’lua’, ’perl’, ’erlang’, ’elixir’,
’c#’, ’csharp’, ’objective-c’, ’clojure’, ’dart’,
]
_STATIC_PATTERNS = [
r’\b\d+\s*/\s*\d+\b’,
# ratios like 4/10, 12/60
r’\b\d+\s*tasks?\b’,
# "60 tasks"
r’\b(small|medium|full|screening)\s*(subset|set|eval|gate)\b’,
r’\bnever\s*(solved|passed|resolved)\b’,
r’\b(ceiling|plateau|peak|floor)\s*(at|of)\s*\d’,
r’\b\d+\s*generation’,
r’/testbed|/exercism’,
# path hints
r’\.(go|py|rs|java|js|cpp|ts|kt|rb|cs)\b’,
# extension hints
]
Every category named in the main paper is covered: task identifiers by the subsets-directory entries,
benchmark names and language names by the two static token lists, and file extensions and evaluation
ratios by the last and first patterns respectively. The remaining patterns cover the “other domain-
revealing” category — task counts, subset names, solved/unsolved language, plateau descriptions,
generation counts and path fragments.
Two modes, deliberately asymmetric.
The policy is built in one of two modes. On the way in, the
aggressive mode blocks every identifier from the subsets directory including the bare exercise name,
even where that name is a common English word. On the way out, the permissive mode keeps the
same static tokens and patterns but narrows the task-name list to distinctive names only, meaning
those containing a hyphen or at least twelve characters, so that an audit is not rejected merely for
suggesting something like “use a counter variable”.
The asymmetry does not open a channel. A short, common-word task name has already been replaced
by DOMAIN on the way in, so the auditor cannot have learned it from the digest; its appearance in the
output would be a coincidence of ordinary English rather than a transfer of task information. Note
that the main paper describes the output check as running against “the same policy”: the static tokens
and patterns are indeed identical, and it is only the task-name list that is narrowed in the manner just
described.
Behaviour on failure.
If the output check fails, the audit is retried once, with the offending phrase
named:
Prompt 7: Auditor. Retry prompt, issued once when the returned text fails the output leak check.
Your previous answer contained a forbidden phrase: {phrase}. Re-write your list of
,→mechanism categories with that phrase removed. Stay strictly domain-agnostic -- no
,→
language names, no task identifiers, no eval discussion.
Original prompt context:
17


--- Page 18 ---
{prompt}
Re-write the numbered list now.
If the retry also fails, the audit is discarded and no new directive is written. The previously cached
valid directive is retained and continues to be supplied, as in Algorithm 1, so a leaking audit never
reaches the meta-agent, and a failed audit does not by itself remove guidance that was already in
force. The loader also fails soft: if the subsets directory is missing or unreadable, the static tokens and
patterns still apply but per-task identifiers are not added; the directory was present for every reported
run. The lookup path is the Polyglot subsets directory, so the per-task identifier list is populated from
Polyglot’s task names, and for the other domains the policy rests on the static token and pattern lists
alone. That is sufficient there because the digest carries diffs of the two agent source files rather than
task data, so domain task identifiers have no route into it in the first place.
Verification over all runs.
We checked this against the artifacts rather than only asserting it.
Rebuilding the forbidden set from Polyglot’s 60 task identifiers and running the shipped leak_check
over every audit directive produced across all runs — 34 directives — returns clean under the output
policy in every case, and none of the 60 identifiers appears in any directive. The two apparent matches
under the stricter input policy, counter and accumulate, are the ordinary English words inside
phrases such as “generate counter-examples” and happen to coincide with exercise names; this is
exactly the common-word collision the permissive output mode is built to tolerate. That result is what
the construction predicts rather than something the output filter had to rescue: the digest is assembled
from scrubbed diff text plus a mechanism type and a signed delta, and carries no description, no
domain field, no absolute score and no task text, so there is no route by which a task name could
reach the auditor in the first place. Applying the same search to all 812 Polyglot records finds no
task identifier in them either, although those records are written after evaluation and are deliberately
tagged with their domain and signed delta — they are the failure-aware memory, not part of the
blindness claim.
B.6
Post-Hoc Record Classifier
Two fields of every record — its mechanism type and its one-line description — are not written by the
meta-agent but assigned afterwards by a separate classifier call over the diff. The main paper names
this component in its limitations as an LLM post-hoc classifier that we do not independently validate;
this section documents it, because the same six-label vocabulary it assigns also drives type-diverse
retrieval and the unexplored-directions hint of Prompt 4.
Label
Definition
prompt_engineering
Changes to system prompts, instructions, or personas
tool_creation
Adding new tools or capabilities
memory_system
Adding performance tracking, history, or knowledge bases
evaluation_logic
Changes to how the meta agent evaluates performance
self_modification
Meta agent changing its own improvement logic
structural_refactor
Reorganizing code without functional change
Table 7: The fixed mechanism-type vocabulary. Every record carries exactly one of these six labels.
The classification prompt is sent as the system message, with the diff supplied as the user message.
The {types} field is filled with the six labels and definitions of Table 7, one per line.
Prompt 8: Classifier. Mechanism-type classification prompt, sent as the system message.
You are a code change classifier. Given a unified diff, classify it into exactly one
,→strategy type:
{types}
18


--- Page 19 ---
IMPORTANT: If a diff modifies BOTH instruction text AND parsing/scoring/validation logic,
,→classify based on which change is MORE SUBSTANTIAL. Adding regex fallbacks,
,→response normalization, score thresholds, or structured output extraction counts
,→as evaluation_logic, NOT prompt_engineering. Only classify as prompt_engineering
,→if the change is PURELY to the wording of instructions or system prompts.
Respond with ONLY the strategy type key (e.g., "prompt_engineering"). Nothing else.
Prompt 9: Classifier. Description prompt. Its output becomes the record’s mechanism description,
the text a later meta-agent actually reads.
Given this diff of a meta-agent modification (classified as "{strategy_type}"), write a
,→1-2 sentence description of what the change does and why it might improve
,→performance.
Diff:
‘‘‘
{diff}
‘‘‘
Respond with ONLY the description. No preamble.
Configuration and failure behaviour.
Both calls run at temperature 0.0 with a 60-second timeout,
capped at 50 output tokens for classification and 200 for description. Three separate paths return
the label structural_refactor without an error being surfaced: an empty diff, a reply that is
not one of the six labels, and any exception during the call. A failed description call is replaced
by a placeholder string. Because classification failures are absorbed into a single label rather than
marked as unknown, the share of the pool labelled structural_refactor should be read as an
upper bound, and any perturbation of the type distribution propagates into type-diverse retrieval and
the unexplored-directions hint. This is the concrete form taken by the unvalidated-classifier limitation
noted in the main paper.
C
Admissibility Gate and Candidate Selection
This section gives the concrete definitions behind the deterministic gate and the selection step de-
scribed under “Proposal Generation, Selection, and Update” in the main paper. Both are implemented
programmatically; no learned model takes part in either.
Editable surface and size band.
The gate checks the two agent source files, and treats a diff as
“modest” only inside a fixed line band:
ALLOWED_FILES
= ("task_agent.py", "meta_agent.py")
MIN_LINES_CHANGED = 5
MAX_LINES_CHANGED = 300
Auxiliary files that a meta-agent may incidentally create (byte-code, notes, helper modules) are
not scored: the raw diff is first filtered down to the allowed files, so such files cannot cause a false
rejection. Only the scope check reads the unfiltered diff, and it passes whenever at least one allowed
file is modified. Auxiliary files are therefore applied to the child agent without being compiled or
counted towards the size band; Sec. G.4 gives an admitted patch that created new helper modules this
way. The gate is a sanity filter on the agent sources, not a containment boundary over every file a
patch touches.
The four gate axes.
Each axis is an independent predicate over one candidate unified diff, and
corresponds directly to the applicability, permitted-scope, compilation and bounded-size checks
named in the main paper.
19


--- Page 20 ---
Function
Returns
Passes when
scope_ok(diff)
{0, 1}
the diff modifies at least one allowed file
applies(diff, repo)
{0, 1}
git apply --check succeeds against the parent
repository, i.e. the patch is applicable without altering the
working tree
compiles_after(diff,
repo)
{0, 1}
the allowed files, copied into a scratch repository with the
diff applied, all pass python -m py_compile
size_band(diff)
{0, 1}
added plus removed lines fall within
[MIN_LINES_CHANGED, MAX_LINES_CHANGED]
Table 8: The four axes of the admissibility gate.
Composition.
The axes combine multiplicatively, so failing any single axis rejects the candidate
outright:
score = applies * scope_ok * compiles_after * size_band
Evaluation short-circuits in the order scope, applicability, compilation, so an out-of-scope diff never
reaches the compiler. Alongside the score, the gate returns a per-axis breakdown together with the
number of lines changed and the list of files modified, which is logged for every generation.
Selection among the K candidates.
The selector has the following signature:
select_best_diff(diff_paths: list[str],
repo_root: str,
tie_break_seed: int = 0) -> tuple[str | None, dict]
Each of the K candidate diffs produced by the parallel meta-agents is scored and the highest scorer is
applied. If every candidate scores zero, the call returns no winner: that generation produces no child,
and both the archive and the strategy pool carry over unchanged.
Because all four axes are binary, the composite score is itself binary — every admissible candidate
scores exactly 1 and every inadmissible one scores 0. There is consequently no quality ordering
among admissible candidates; the winner is drawn from them by a seeded choice. This is the precise
sense in which a learned judge is kept out of the loop: nothing between a proposal and its measured
outcome estimates how good that proposal is, so all quality signal comes from evaluation.
Tie-breaking and its reproducibility.
The draw is seeded from the generation index: the selector
is invoked with the current generation as its tie-break seed, so each generation of a run has a
fixed, non-arbitrary seed rather than an incidental one. That index is then passed through Python’s
hash() applied to a string built from it. Because Python salts hash() for string inputs unless
PYTHONHASHSEED is set, and the repository does not set it, the draw is deterministic within a single
process but not identical across processes.
The consequence is bounded but real. Re-running a configuration reproduces the admissible set at
each generation, and reproduces which candidates tie, but not necessarily which of the tied candidates
is applied — so an exactly identical trajectory is not guaranteed. Seeding the generator with the
integer index directly, instead of with the hash of a string built from it, would remove this. We
therefore do not claim cross-process reproducibility for the identity of the tie-break winner. In
proportion, it is a minor source of run-to-run variation beside sampling from the language models
themselves, which is stochastic at every non-zero temperature.
20


--- Page 21 ---
D
Computing Infrastructure
The cost of these experiments is dominated by calls to hosted language models rather than by local
computation. The meta-agents, the task agents, the auditor and the record classifier are all API calls;
local machines run the evolution loop and the containerised evaluation harnesses, and train policies
for the robotics reward-design domain. Compute is therefore accounted for in tokens, as in Table 1 of
the main paper, rather than in GPU-hours.
Component

Table 9: Computing infrastructure used for the reported experiments.
The robotics reward-design domain ran on the GPU nodes, because scoring a generated reward
function requires training a locomotion policy locally. The other four domains ran on the CPU
nodes, where local work is limited to the evolution loop and the containerised evaluation harnesses.
Simulator and reinforcement-learning dependencies for the robotics domain are pinned separately in
the accompanying requirements files, with PyTorch installed against a CUDA index in the container
image.
E
Randomization and Run Protocol
The run protocol is inherited from DGM-Hyperagents. Every configuration is executed as five
repeated runs, and results are reported as medians with bootstrap confidence intervals over those five.
A run is a complete evolutionary trajectory starting from the same initial agent, not a re-evaluation of
a single trajectory, so the spread across runs reflects variation in the search itself rather than evaluation
noise.
Which baseline numbers we ran.
This protocol covers every run we executed. The DGM-H
numbers for paper review, robotics reward design and the three IMO-grading settings are not among
them: their scores, intervals and generations-to-best are taken as published by Zhang et al. [2026], on
the same datasets, splits, models and evaluators, and were not rerun. Those baseline runs did not pass
through our admissibility gate (Sec. C). For Polyglot and audit risk we ran the baseline ourselves, as
MetaShare with the strategy pool disabled and a single meta-agent (k=1) behind the same gate, five
runs each; these two domains are the controlled comparisons.
What is randomized within a run.
Parent selection is stochastic and follows DGM-Hyperagents
unchanged. Each archived agent ai carries a novelty term hi = 1/(1 + ni), where ni is the number
of children already generated from it, and an unnormalized weight wi = sihi that combines the
agent’s score with that term. The weights are normalized into a categorical distribution — uniform
if they sum to zero — and parents are drawn from it independently with replacement. Selection
therefore prefers strong agents without committing to them, and discounts agents that have already
been expanded.
21


--- Page 22 ---
Decoding is stochastic in all but one slot: of the K parallel meta-agents the first decodes greedily
at temperature 0.0, and the remainder sample at the temperatures listed in Table 5. Ties in the
admissibility gate are broken by a draw seeded from the generation index, as described in Sec. C.
What differs between runs, and the limits of replay.
The five runs of a configuration differ only
in these draws. The initial agent, the domain and its splits, the iteration budget, and every setting in
Sec. A are held fixed. For the ablations the same five run configurations are reused across arms, which
is what makes those comparisons paired: each arm sees the same sequence of random conditions, so
a difference between arms is attributable to the component toggled rather than to run-to-run luck.
Exact replay of a run is nevertheless not achievable, and we do not claim it. Two sources are outside
our control or not seed-determined: sampling from hosted language models at non-zero temperature,
which is not reproducible from a seed on the client side, and the tie-break draw discussed in Sec. C.
What is reproducible is the protocol — the number of runs, the selection rule, the staged gate, and the
settings of Sec. A — and the aggregate behaviour those produce, which is why we report medians
with intervals over five runs rather than single trajectories.
F
Financial Audit-Risk Dataset
F.1
Inherent Risk Factor Definitions
Each account is assessed against the fifteen inherent risk factors listed below. Throughout this table
“account” is shorthand for the account group that carries the assessment; the (client, IRF) pair of
the main paper is the decision cell that these group-level assessments realise, as set out under “Unit
of counting” in Sec. F.2. Twelve are general factors that apply to any account; the twelfth of these,
accounting estimates, records whether the account is or contains an accounting estimate, and a
positive determination brings the final three estimate-specific factors into scope. The factors follow
an established audit risk-assessment framework, and are named and summarised here at the level of
the underlying concept rather than reproduced verbatim; the response options, the ranking scale and
the weighting used to combine them belong to that framework and are not redistributed.
22


--- Page 23 ---

F.2
Labelling Protocol and Class Balance
Labels were assigned by qualified audit practitioners in the course of engagement work, following the
guidance of the risk-assessment framework; they were not produced by the authors and not produced
by a model. Each (account, factor) pair carries one of three levels: High, Medium or None. The
framework also distinguishes a fourth, lower ranking, which does not appear as a label class in this
corpus, so every label in the corpus falls into one of those three.
The labels themselves, and the per-factor assessments they derive from, are client confidential and
are not released. We report only aggregate accuracy, normalized mean absolute error, and accuracy
broken down by factor.
No assessment was double-labelled or adjudicated, so no inter-annotator agreement figure is available:
each label is the judgement recorded by the practitioner responsible for that engagement. Accuracy
against these labels therefore measures agreement with a single expert judgement rather than with an
adjudicated ground truth, which is the sense in which the main paper describes the metric.
The distribution is heavily skewed: None accounts for roughly 72% of all labels, and High and
Medium together for the remaining 28%. This is the reason the main paper reports normalized mean
absolute error and per-factor accuracy alongside overall accuracy — a predictor that answered None
everywhere would score well on accuracy alone while carrying no useful risk signal.
Unit of counting.
Two levels of granularity are in play, and the main paper and Table 11 report
different ones. The coarser level is the decision grid, which is what the main paper counts: fifteen
23


--- Page 24 ---
Split
Clients
High
Medium
None
Total

8

2344
3221

2
132
127
506
765

15

single account group against a single factor.
clients, each assessed against all fifteen inherent risk factors, giving the 15 × 15 = 225 (client, IRF)
pairs quoted there, of which the five test clients supply 5 × 15 = 75 decisions. The finer level is
the stored label. A client’s accounts are organised into groups, and every group is assessed against
all fifteen factors, so each cell of the decision grid is realised once per account group of the client
in question and the unit of a label is a (client, group, factor) triple. A client contributing n groups
therefore contributes 15n labels, and n varies by client; across the fifteen clients the corpus spans on
the order of 330 account groups.
Table 11 counts at this finer level — 4896 labels in total and 910 in the test split, against the 225
and 75 decisions of the grid above. The totals are not exact multiples of fifteen because assessments
falling at the framework’s fourth ranking are excluded, as described above. Accuracy, normalized
mean absolute error and per-factor accuracy are all computed over the group-level labels, so the
figures of 225 and 75 in the main paper describe the space of distinct decisions the task covers rather
than the number of scored predictions behind each reported metric.
F.3
Why a Public Alternative Is Not Sufficient
What the system reads at inference is what the main paper describes: chunks of the Financial Notes of
the client’s annual filing, supplied together with the inherent risk factor to be assessed. What cannot
be rebuilt from public sources is everything around that input. The task pairs two things that are not
jointly available in public form: account-level financial detail, and a per-factor risk level assigned
by a practitioner. The filings themselves are public documents, but the account-level trial balance
that determines which account groups exist, and therefore which assessments are in scope, is not;
neither are the practitioner assessments that serve as labels. Releasing either would disclose client
information, so the corpus is not released and the reported numbers are aggregates.
No public benchmark substitutes. Financial-NLP corpora built on public filings target retrieval,
question answering or sentiment, and none of them attaches a standardized set of inherent risk factors,
at account granularity, labelled by practitioners applying a consistent framework. A public corpus
could therefore only approximate the surface form of the task, not the judgement being evaluated,
which is precisely the property that makes this a document-grounded transfer test rather than another
classification benchmark. That is also why we report it as a fifth domain testing transfer, and why the
paper’s claims for it rest on aggregate metrics and on the comparison against the same baseline under
the same protocol, rather than on reproducibility of the corpus itself.
F.4
Per-Run Results and Reporting Convention
The main paper states a single reporting convention — medians over five runs with bootstrap intervals
— and one statistic on this domain departs from it, so we state that exception explicitly here. Accuracy
is reported as the median over runs, as the paper describes and as used for the other domains.
Normalized mean absolute error is the exception: it is reported as the mean. The distinction matters
only for the baseline, whose first run attains an unusually low error: taking medians instead would
give 0.369 against 0.305, a gap of 0.064 rather than the 0.045 we report, so the mean is the more
conservative choice for our comparison.
F.5

Table 13 breaks accuracy down over the fifteen factors, in the order of Table 10. Each entry is the
median over the five runs.

The aggregate improvement is not uniform, and the breakdown is the more informative result. Three
factors account for most of the gain, and all three require reading the narrative disclosure rather than
counting entries: transaction homogeneity (+0.55), fraud indicators (+0.53) and the presence of an
accounting estimate (+0.45). A second group improves more modestly — reporting complexity and
related-party transactions (+0.20 each), contingent liabilities (+0.17) and transaction complexity
(+0.14). Two factors are saturated for both systems, which reflects a near-degenerate label distribution
for those factors rather than a modelling result.
Two factors regress clearly: loss exposure (−0.54) and transaction volume (−0.25). The shared
memory therefore shifts where the agent is competent rather than lifting every factor at once, and
we report the breakdown rather than the aggregate alone because that shift is the more accurate
description of what the memory does in this domain. It also suggests a limit worth stating: the
mechanism transfers judgement that can be argued from the text of a disclosure, and does not help —
and here actively hurts — on factors that depend on quantities the narrative does not contain.
G
Polyglot: Per-Run Detail
G.1
Results Across the Five Runs
The main paper reports a median of 0.917 with a 95% bootstrap CI of [0.900, 0.933] over five repeated
runs, reached within ten iterations. Table 14 gives the runs behind that summary; with five runs the
bootstrap distribution of the median is supported on the observed values, so the interval’s endpoints
fall on run values rather than between them. To match GEA’s model configuration these runs use
Claude Sonnet-4.5 as both task- and meta-agent, which differs from the GPT o3-mini task-agent used
25


--- Page 26 ---
everywhere else in our Polyglot results; numbers here are therefore not comparable with the o3-mini
results in Sec. G.3 or with the main paper’s Polyglot ablation. Matching the models does not match
the initialisation, as the third limit in Sec. G.2 sets out.

G.2
Comparison with GEA
On the same 60-task small+medium subset, GEA reports 0.88 and DGM 0.683 [Weng et al., 2026].
Our median of 0.917 and best run of 0.933 sit above both, and our runs reach their best within ten
iterations against roughly thirty for GEA’s final plateau. Figure 4 places the trajectories side by side.

Figure 4: Best score so far against evolution iteration on the 60-task small+medium Polyglot subset.
The MetaShare curve is the best of our five runs, ending at 0.933; the median over the five is 0.917
(Table 14). The DGM and GEA curves are digitised from the published figure in Weng et al. [2026]:
plateau levels and the iterations at which they begin were read off the plot, so they are approximate
and indicate shape rather than exact values. Dashed line: reported open-source state of the art. Note
that the initialisations differ—both baselines begin from an agent already scoring ≈0.38, whereas
MetaShare begins from an agent that solves nothing.
Three limits should be read alongside that figure, and together they are why the main paper describes
this as competitive at a lower iteration count rather than as a win.
First, the comparison is not like-for-like on variance. GEA reports a single-run point estimate, so
there is no interval to compare against our five-run spread, and we cannot tell whether 0.88 is a
typical or a fortunate run of that system. A gap of 0.037 (about two of the 60 tasks) between our
median and a single unrepeated number is not evidence of a reliable ordering.
26


--- Page 27 ---
Second, the baseline curves are digitised rather than reproduced. We did not re-run GEA or DGM;
we read their plateaus off the published figure. That is enough to compare the shape of the trajectories
and the iteration at which each plateaus, but the individual values carry reading error, and small
differences between the curves should not be interpreted.
Third, the runs do not share an initialisation. The main paper’s “matching that configuration” refers
to the models each system runs; the starting agent is not matched. GEA and DGM are seeded with an
agent that already solves roughly 38% of the subset, while our agent starts at zero and must discover
every capability the curve shows. This difference runs against us in the final-score comparison,
since our system covers the same ground from further back, but it also means the two curves are
not measuring the same quantity over the same interval: the early part of our trajectory is capability
acquisition, whereas for the baselines it is refinement of an already competent agent.
G.3
Task Coverage Across Generations
Peak accuracy is a property of a single checkpoint, and it can hide what the search actually did. Two
runs can solve the same number of tasks in every generation and still differ in whether those are
the same tasks each time or different ones; only the second is exploring. We therefore also report
cumulative unique tasks solved: we take each generation, record which coding tasks its agent solves,
and count the distinct tasks solved at any point in the run, over the 60-task small+medium subset of
the 225-task Polyglot benchmark. Because it accumulates over the whole run and is insensitive to
how often a task is re-solved, this quantity measures the variety the population reaches rather than the
quality of one endpoint, and it upper-bounds the task set of any individual checkpoint. It is a different
measurement from the best-so-far accuracy in the main paper’s Polyglot ablation, which is taken on
the full 225-task benchmark at the best-performing generation; the two are not commensurable and
should not be read against each other.
Both arms receive the same 100-generation budget and the same staged evaluation protocol, and in
both the task-agent runs on GPT o3-mini for the whole run, with Claude Sonnet-4.5 as meta-agent.
This is also what the caption of Figure 3 of the main paper means by holding the task-agent on
o3-mini for Polyglot: the runs reported there are ones in which the task-agent remained on o3-mini
for the whole run, not ones in which switching was disabled. Model switching is in the action space
of both arms, as elsewhere on this domain, and was neither forced nor blocked in either of them;
the five MetaShare runs reported here are ones in which the meta-agent did not exercise it, so the
coverage comparison isolates the search rather than a difference in task-agent backbone. The runs in
which routing does emerge are traced separately in Sec. G.4 and are not counted here, so this table
understates the full system rather than flattering it.
