Table 15: Cumulative unique Polyglot tasks solved per run, out of the 60-task small+medium subset,
over a matched 100-generation budget.
MetaShare covers more tasks in every run, and the two sets of run outcomes do not overlap: the
baseline spans 21–22 tasks while MetaShare spans 24–27. The median rises from 21 to 27 of the
60 tasks, a relative increase of 1.29× on medians and 1.22× on means. The separation is small in
absolute terms but consistent, and it is not bought with extra generations: both arms run the full 100
generations, and MetaShare’s best checkpoint arrives well before that budget is exhausted.
We read this as evidence for the mechanism rather than for the headline score. Under failure-aware
sharing, a branch that has recorded a dead end does not need to rediscover it, and the signed records
make that dead end legible to genealogically distant branches; the search therefore spends its budget
27


--- Page 28 ---
on tasks it has not yet attacked instead of re-attempting known-bad mechanisms. Coverage is the
measurement where that effect should appear most directly, since it rewards reaching new tasks rather
than refining an existing solution. Two caveats bound the claim. The counts are per-run and not
pooled, so they are not a union over the five runs and should not be added. And coverage credits a
task solved at any generation, so it does not certify that the finally selected checkpoint solves all of
the tasks counted.
G.4
Emergent Dynamic Model Selection
The main paper reports that on Polyglot the auditor unlocks a capability rather than an incremental
gain: the meta-agent discovers that it can change the task-agent’s model, which DGM-H never
proposes despite having the same action available. This section traces that episode through one
Polyglot run that begins on GPT o3-mini and leaves it at generation 20, from the search collapse that
triggered the audit to the modification that followed. The directive and pool digest reproduced below
are one sample, drawn from a single audit in that run and shown for reference; both the categories
proposed and the records retrieved differ across runs and across audits within a run.
The search collapses before this audit.
The audit traced here is the one that fires at generation 20,
over a pool of nineteen records; under the cadence C of Table 4 it need not be the first audit of the
run, and it is singled out because its directive is the one the meta-agents then acted on. Table 16
summarises the mechanism types the classifier assigned to the pool records of this run. Over the
first nineteen generations the population produced exactly two of the six mechanism types, and the
concentration is stronger than those counts suggest: generations 10 through 19 are ten consecutive
records that all implement self-consistency decoding, contributed by seven distinct lineages. This is
the failure mode the auditor exists to detect, and it is a population-level failure rather than one branch
getting stuck — independent lineages converged on the same recipe. Every one of the nineteen
records carries a performance delta of 0.000: the run had not yet solved anything.

Table 16: Mechanism types in the pool of one Polyglot run that begins on GPT o3-mini, before and
after the generation-20 audit fired. Types are assigned by the post-hoc classifier of Sec. B.6; the six
available types are listed in Table 7.
The directive.
The auditor sees the nineteen diffs, with evaluation content removed by the scrubbing
of Sec. B.5, and returns the text in Prompt 10. It names the redundancy it found and proposes eight
absent categories. Nothing in the returned text refers to a task, a test case, or a score; the reasoning is
entirely about the shape of the diffs it was shown.
Prompt 10: Auditor. Directive returned by the auditor for this run, verbatim. Dynamic Model
Selection is the first of eight proposed categories. Shown as one sample directive; the categories
proposed vary between audits.
Looking at the 19 diffs, I see heavy emphasis on prompt engineering and
self-consistency voting mechanisms, but several important categories are
missing or under-represented:
1. **Dynamic Model Selection**
- Automatically switches between different models or model configurations
based on task characteristics or intermediate results. Introduces model
routing logic and performance tracking across model variants.
28


--- Page 29 ---
2. **Hierarchical Problem Decomposition**
- Breaks complex tasks into subtasks with recursive solving and result
composition. Structurally different by introducing task splitting
functions and dependency management between subtask solutions.
3. **Memory-Based Learning from Failures**
- Maintains persistent storage of past failures and successful strategies
to inform future attempts. Adds failure pattern recognition and strategy
adaptation based on historical performance data.
4. **Multi-Agent Collaboration**
- Uses multiple specialized agent instances with different roles (e.g.,
critic, solver, validator) that interact to reach solutions. Introduces
agent coordination protocols and role-based reasoning chains.
5. **Adaptive Timeout and Resource Management**
- Dynamically adjusts computation time, tool usage limits, or reasoning
depth based on task complexity and available resources. Adds resource
monitoring and adaptive constraint adjustment mechanisms.
6. **Iterative Solution Refinement**
- Generates initial solutions then systematically improves them through
multiple refinement cycles. Introduces solution evolution loops and
incremental improvement tracking, distinct from simple retry logic.
7. **Confidence-Weighted Ensemble Methods**
- Combines multiple solution approaches using learned confidence weights
rather than simple voting. Adds confidence calibration and weighted
aggregation beyond basic consensus mechanisms.
8. **Dynamic Prompt Optimization**
- Automatically modifies prompts based on intermediate results or detected
failure modes. Introduces prompt mutation and selection mechanisms that
evolve during execution.
How the directive reaches the meta-agent.
Prompt 11 shows the assembled context, with the
directive at the top as a mandatory instruction and the pool digest below it as reference material. Three
features of the assembly are visible here. The directive is cached: the text says “the 19 diffs” while
the digest beneath it already contains the generation-20 record, because the audit output is carried
forward until the next audit fires rather than regenerated every generation. The success and failure
blocks are separate, and only one positive record appears because only one existed — the retrieval
budget Ks is an upper bound, not a quota. The failure block’s heading is the implementation’s
own wording, and it names both cases: the operative criterion is the non-positive test δi ≤0, so
records with δi = 0.000 appear there as strategies that did not work rather than as ones that reduced
performance. And the unexplored-directions footer is computed from the classifier’s type inventory,
so it lists the two types still absent from the pool at that point.
Prompt 11: Auditor. Assembled meta-agent context in a generation after the routing change was
recorded. Strategy bodies are elided where they repeat; the directive block is the cached output of
Prompt 10. Shown as one sample context.
--- MUST TRY: mechanism categories absent from all prior strategies (eval-blind audit) ---
You MUST attempt one of the categories below. Do not produce another variation
of the recipes shown later -- that path has plateaued.
[the eight-category directive above is reproduced here verbatim]
--- PRIOR STRATEGIES (reference only -- do NOT clone the dominant recipe) ---
[Strategy 1] +0.500 on polyglot (gen_20, branch 13):
This change adds a dynamic model routing system that analyzes task
characteristics to automatically select the most appropriate language model
29


--- Page 30 ---
for each task, then tracks performance metrics (success rate and execution
time) to improve future model selection decisions. [...]
--- STRATEGIES THAT REDUCED PERFORMANCE or DID NOT WORK (avoid these approaches)---
[Strategy 2] +0.000 on polyglot (gen_1, branch 0):
This change enhances the meta-agent’s self-improvement by providing it with
concrete guidance on what code areas to modify (task agent, tools, LLM
integration, etc.) and incorporating recent evaluation results as context
for deciding what improvements to make. [...]
[Strategy 3] +0.000 on polyglot (gen_2, branch 0):
This change enhances the agent’s prompt by adding explicit identity framing
("capable problem-solving agent"), encouraging step-by-step reasoning [...]
[Strategies 4-6: three further prompt-scaffolding variants, gen_3, gen_5, gen_6]
--- UNEXPLORED STRATEGY DIRECTIONS: memory_system, self_modification ---
What the meta-agents proposed.
In the generation following the audit, all three parallel
meta-agents abandoned the self-consistency recipe and each targeted a category from the di-
rective.
Two proposed Dynamic Model Selection, creating agent/model_router.py and
agent/model_selector.py respectively; the third proposed Hierarchical Problem Decomposition,
creating agent/task_decomposer.py. All three cleared every axis of the admissibility gate of
Sec. C with a composite score of 1.0, so the three-way tie was resolved by the generation-seeded
tie-break draw of Sec. C, which in this generation selected the first candidate. The resulting record
is the only positive entry in the run’s pool, moving the score from 0.000 to 0.500. That score is
the training-time score of this single run on the 60-task small+medium subset, which is what the
evolution loop scores against; it is neither an aggregate over the five runs nor a figure on the 225-task
benchmark, so it should not be read against the Polyglot accuracies of the main paper. It is also
measured after the routing change, with GPT 4o-mini serving the tasks, so it is not comparable with
the coverage counts of Sec. G.3 either, which come from runs whose task-agent stays on o3-mini
throughout.
What the modification actually does.
The selected patch adds a router that classifies each task
and selects the model the task-agent runs it on, recording per-model success rate and execution time
to inform later routing. In this run the router sent Polyglot tasks to GPT 4o-mini, so in practice
the task-agent moved off o3-mini to GPT 4o-mini and stayed there — exactly the model change
the main paper reports. The original model is restored after each task, so o3-mini survives as the
fallback default when the router declines to route. This upgrade is the task-agent model change that
the main paper identifies as an uncontrolled difference between the arms on this domain, and the
control reported there applies unchanged: the runs that stay on o3-mini throughout still beat the
DGM-H baseline in fewer iterations.
Contrast and caveats.
DGM-H has the same action available and does not take it in any run, which
is the observation the ablation rests on. One limit applies: the episode above is a single run traced
in detail, offered as a mechanism account rather than as evidence of frequency; the reproducibility
claim rests on the ablation arms, not on this trace.
30
